commonsFile: File:Ziggurat of Ur Site in Nasiriyah 03.jpg
attribution: Alli Khalil — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The restored Ziggurat of Ur, a stepped mudbrick temple tower, rising above flat desert plain under blue sky
caption: The Ziggurat of Ur, built around 2100 BCE for the moon god Nanna and partly restored in the 20th century. It is the southern anchor of the Sumerian leg, a short drive from the Chibayish marshes.

attribution: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg) — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Reconstructed mudbrick walls and archways of ancient Babylon on a sunny day
caption: Babylon's reconstructed brick walls, a Wiki Loves Monuments record of the Neo-Babylonian city of Nebuchadnezzar II. It is the first great ancient site south of Baghdad on the route to Najaf.

attribution: Unknown author Unknown author — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: A Marsh Arab poling a narrow mashoof canoe through reed-lined water in the Chibayish marshes
caption: A Marsh Arab poles a mashoof canoe through the Ahwar near Chibayish, part of a UNESCO mixed World Heritage property. Travelling by canoe to reed-house villages is the trip's living-culture counterpart to the ruins of Ur and Uruk.

attribution: Mondalawy — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Al-Mutanabbi Street in Baghdad at night, with lit bookstalls and crowds
caption: Al-Mutanabbi Street, Baghdad's historic booksellers' quarter, lit up at night. It is the opening walk of the Baghdad days, where the city's intellectual life is most visible.

attribution: jan kurdistani — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Aerial view of the Erbil Citadel, a raised oval mound of ochre walls in the middle of the modern city
caption: The Erbil Citadel, a tell crowning the middle of the city and among the longest continuously inhabited places on Earth. It opens the Kurdistan Region section of the route.

attribution: Khoshhat — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Steep limestone walls of the Rawanduz canyon in the Kurdistan mountains
caption: The Rawanduz (Gali Ali Beg) canyon in the Kurdistan Region, the route's big mountain landscape. It is the scenic day between the Erbil Citadel and the Amedi highlands.

commonsFile: File:Shrine of Imam Ali Najaf August 2023.jpg
attribution: Goudarz.memar — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Golden dome and courtyard of the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf
caption: The golden-domed Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf, one of the principal Shia pilgrimage sites. It stands for the religious heritage leg with Karbala, between Babylon and the southern Sumerian sites.

attribution: Chris Hoare — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The spiral Malwiya minaret of the Great Mosque of Samarra rising above the plain
caption: The 9th-century spiral Malwiya minaret in Samarra, a UNESCO-listed Abbasid capital. It is the northern Baghdad-region day trip that shows Iraq's early Islamic golden age.

commonsFile: File:Views around Sirsing (near Amedi, in Duhok Governorate) 01.jpg
attribution: Levi Clancy — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Green mountain valley with villages near Amedi in Kurdistan
caption: Green mountain country at Sirsing near Amedi in Duhok Governorate. The Amedi highlands are the cool, hiking-friendly end point of the Kurdistan Region leg.

attribution: المكتب الاعلامي لرئيس الوزراء — CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Golden domes and minarets of the Al-Kadhimiya Mosque in Baghdad
caption: The golden domes and minarets of the Al-Kadhimiya Mosque, one of Baghdad's major Shia shrines. It is the religious-heritage stop in the capital, alongside Al-Mutanabbi Street and the Iraq Museum.

attribution: Karbobala.com — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Gold-domed shrine of Al-Abbas in Karbala against the sky
caption: The Al-Abbas shrine in Karbala, one of the two great shrine cities of the pilgrimage circuit. The route passes it with Najaf to understand the scale of Iraqi Shia religious life.

commonsFile: File:Courtyard of the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, Iraq.jpg
attribution: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg) — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Courtyard of the Iraq Museum in Baghdad
caption: The courtyard of the Iraq Museum, home of the finest Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian collections. It is the museum stop in Baghdad that gives context for the sites seen later in the south.

attribution: Levi Clancy — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Crowded covered market alley of the Erbil bazaar
caption: The old bazaar at the foot of the Erbil Citadel, with traders selling spices, clothes and household goods. It is where the Kurdistan leg is most about everyday life rather than monuments.
